claims.text: Wear performance is governed by the formation of a continuous, thermally stable spinel oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.
The protective spinel oxide can have the nominal composition (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4.
A continuous protective oxide layer forms preferentially in coatings having an equiatomic, homogeneous elemental distribution.
The continuous spinel oxide layer acts as a barrier to mechanical wear.
The initial Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 microwave-cladded coating on SS-304 has a uniform, equiatomic microstructure.
Increasing Fe to 30 at.% while reducing Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu to 17.5 at.% each will disrupt uniform protective-oxide formation.
Oxide formation is expected during sliding near 800 °C, 2 m/s, 15 N, and 1000 m.
At high temperature, selective oxidation of the homogeneous equiatomic coating uniformly forms a protective spinel film.
The protective oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact lowers the wear rate.
Disrupting the elemental balance impedes development of a uniform oxide layer and thereby increases wear.
The balanced equiatomic coating will have a lower wear rate than the compositionally imbalanced coating.
The balanced equiatomic coating will exhibit a more stable friction coefficient than the imbalanced coating.
The imbalanced coating will exhibit less continuous oxide coverage than the balanced coating.
Under the stated test conditions, the equiatomic baseline coating exhibits a wear rate of about 0.0018 mm3/m.
The equiatomic baseline coating forms a continuous protective oxide layer after high-temperature exposure.
The proposed effect should hold near 800 °C for compositions similar to Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Cu under the stated sliding and load conditions.
Secondary intermetallic phases may also affect wear performance.
